title: The three robbers
hookLine: Ramakrishna's three robbers in a forest, and the Gita's field marks for each guna
carry: tamas strikes, rajas binds, sattva shows the road
last: NATURE IS WOVEN OF THREE GUNAS.

cards: Ramakrishna, the nineteenth-century saint of Bengal, told this one. A traveler is crossing a forest when three robbers jump him and take everything. The first says: why keep him alive? and reaches for his knife.
The second says: no, just tie him up. They tie him and walk off. Later the third comes back alone, unties him, says sorry, and walks him to the main road.
That's your way home, he says. Come with me, the traveler begs. I can't, says the robber.
The police would know me. The forest, Ramakrishna said, is this world. The three robbers are the gunas.

teach.b: In the Gita, Krishna gives Arjuna the field marks of the same three. Verse ten: one thread rises by pushing down the other two, so the mix is always shifting.
Verse eleven: when light and understanding shine through every gate of the body, the eyes, the ears, the mind, sattva is strong.
Verse twelve: greed, busyness, starting one project after another, restlessness, longing: that's rajas rising. Verse thirteen: darkness, sluggishness, carelessness, confusion: that's tamas.
Verse seventeen follows each to where it leads: from sattva, knowledge; from rajas, greed; from tamas, confusion.
Verse eighteen gives a direction: those in sattva rise, those in rajas stay in the middle, those in tamas sink. The chapter even says the thread you're in at the end of life shapes what comes next.
Then verse nineteen: when the seer sees no doer other than the gunas, and knows what is beyond them, that one reaches my being. That's how Ramakrishna read the robbers.
Tamas would destroy you, rajas ties you up, sattva unties you and points to the road, but even the kind robber can't walk you home.
Home is beyond all three. And the first step is noticing: the moment you can say, oh, that's rajas, you're already a little outside it.

how: Some Hindus use the gunas as a practical check on daily life, choosing food, company and routines that support sattva; some teachers use Gita 14.11–14.13 to describe what each guna looks like.

o: a cool, steady patience that waits without wanting
royal power, the kind of authority a king holds
passion and motion, the restless, grasping thread

games.q: the field marks — tap the pairs.
p: sees no doer but the threads

s: in Gita 14, one guna rises by overpowering the other two
verse 10: the mix is always shifting.
the Gita says rajas leads to knowledge
verse 17: sattva leads to knowledge; rajas to greed; tamas to confusion.
verse 19 says the seer sees no doer other than the gunas
the threads move; the one watching isn't a thread.

games.q: in Ramakrishna's story, the third robber unties you and points to the road. why won't he come home with you?
o: he's still a robber: sattva frees you from the other two, but home is beyond all three.
he's angry that you got robbed.
there is no home; the forest is all there is.
games.why: sattva shows the way, but it still binds (Gita 14.6). Ramakrishna said the home is beyond all three gunas, and verse 19 points there too.

practice: Scan yourself for the Gita's field marks. Light and clear seeing, through the eyes and ears: the bright thread. Restlessness, wanting, an itch in the hands to start something new: the moving thread.
Fog, heaviness, a wish to go blank: the heavy one. Whatever is strongest, name it softly, the way Nani might: ah, that's rajas. Then rest as the one who noticed.
The robbers move; the watcher isn't one of them.

wordCard.voice: Rajas, passion, motion, heat: the robber who ties you up. Gita fourteen, twelve: its marks are greed, busyness, starting one thing after another, restlessness and longing.

orig.note: Sanskrit: rajas, passion, motion, heat; the middle thread, whose field marks are greed and restlessness (Gita 14.12).

carryVoice: Your line: tamas strikes, rajas binds, sattva shows the road. Home is beyond all three. Two hundred eight days now.
